title: India Is Preparing to Miss Its Budget Deficit Target for the First Time Since the Pandemic. The Iran War Is the Reason.
excerpt: Bloomberg reports the government will let the fiscal gap widen to 4.8% of GDP — half a percentage point above the February target — as energy subsidies balloon and oil stays above $85 a barrel.
body:
India is preparing to miss its fiscal deficit target for the first time since the pandemic year of 2020-21, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, as the three-month-old war in Iran drives up energy subsidies and squeezes government finances in ways New Delhi can no longer absorb.

Authorities are willing to let the deficit widen by as much as half a percentage point — from the 4.3% of GDP goal set in February's budget to 4.8% — according to an official familiar with the deliberations. The Finance Ministry has already begun briefing credit rating agencies, framing the slippage as a direct consequence of external geopolitical pressures rather than any loosening of fiscal discipline.

## The Oil Arithmetic

The numbers tell a stark story. India imports roughly 90% of its crude oil and is the world's third-largest consumer. Before the Iran war broke out on February 28, Brent crude sat comfortably below $75 a barrel. On Friday, even after a 4% drop on hopes of a peace deal, it was still trading near $87.

Higher crude has forced state oil retailers to raise petrol and diesel prices by about 8% since the conflict began. The government has simultaneously cut subsidies on household cooking gas cylinders — a politically sensitive move that signals just how tight the fiscal space has become. The fertiliser subsidy, another major budget line, is projected to jump 20% this fiscal year.

## What the Rating Agencies Are Watching

The Finance Ministry's outreach to rating agencies is not routine. India currently holds a "Baa3" rating from Moody's with a stable outlook — the lowest investment-grade tier. A missed deficit target, even one attributed to war, could test the confidence that underpins that rating.

Moody's trimmed India's GDP growth forecast to 6% for fiscal 2027, down from 6.8% earlier, and warned in an April report that a prolonged energy disruption could "entrench inflation, strain fiscal and monetary policy flexibility, and test external investor confidence." The World Bank, which upgraded India's growth projection this week to 6.6%, acknowledged the same downside risks.

The government is keeping its options open. Officials plan to reassess the fiscal outlook later this year, once there is more clarity on non-tax revenues — including potential disinvestment proceeds — and the trajectory of subsidy costs. Spending cuts across ministries are also being evaluated, Bloomberg reported.

## The Rupee Connection

The deficit story does not exist in isolation. A wider gap means more government borrowing, which pushes up bond yields and puts additional pressure on the rupee. The currency is already Asia's second-worst performer this year, down 6%, though it rallied to 95.11 against the dollar on Friday after Trump said an Iran deal could be signed as soon as this weekend.

The Reserve Bank of India has been running a parallel operation to shore up the currency. Last week, it announced a subsidised foreign currency swap window for banks, effectively absorbing the hedging cost on three-to-five-year NRI deposits. Banks have responded by raising FCNR(B) deposit rates to as high as 7.1%, hoping to attract $35-40 billion in dollar inflows by September.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, the fiscal slippage cuts both ways. The immediate fear is a weaker rupee — remittances sent home lose value, and rupee-denominated investments deliver lower returns when converted back to dollars or pounds. A sovereign downgrade, however unlikely in the near term, would amplify those losses.

But the new NRI deposit rates — the highest in years — create a window of opportunity. If the deficit stays contained at 4.8% and the Iran conflict winds down, the rupee could recover toward the 93-94 range that Kotak Mahindra Bank projects. Locking in a 7% dollar deposit now, before rates normalise, could prove to be well-timed.

The broader signal is that India's economy, for all its structural momentum — the World Bank upgrade, the $315-billion IT sector, the data centre boom — remains deeply exposed to an oil shock it did not cause and cannot control. The deficit number is just the ledger entry for that exposure.
